topics.title: Efficiency problem
topics.text:
Bob can clean the garage in 9 hrs less time than his brother Paul.  Working together, they can do the job in 20 hrs. How long would it take each one to do the job alone?



This is my work so far:

let $p$ equal to Paul's efficiency

Bob does $\dfrac{1}{p-9}$ of the work in one hour

Paul does $\dfrac{1}{p}$ of the work in one hour

$\dfrac{1}{p}$ $+$ $\dfrac{1}{p-9}$ $=$ $\dfrac{1}{20}$

I think this was where I went wrong.

I solved it and ended with

$p^2$ $-$ $49p$ $+$ $180$ $=$ $0$

Are the steps right?

topics.title: Using 1-5-5-7 to Create 1-100
topics.text:
Some fun with simple operations...

Using the numbers 1, 5, 5, and 7, create all the integers from 1 to 100 using the four basic arithmetic operations and, if needed, decimal points, exponents, and the square root sign. The four numbers must all be used once and only once each time in expressing the hundred integers. For example, 80 = 17 x 5 - 5, and 16 = 75 / 5 +1.

Personally, I have been able to do so for all but twelve numbers; for the missing dozen, I have had to resort to factorial notation and, in one case, the repeating-bar symbol used with decimals. These solutions are quite interesting, but they do not meet the original criteria.

The twelve difficult ones are: 46, 66, 67, 78, 83, 87, 89, 91, 92, 94, 97, and 99. For example, 99 = 75 + (5-1)! - so how can 99 be expressed without the factorial sign?

Can anyone solve any of "The Dirty Dozen" without factorials or repeating bars?

And let me know if anyone wants a solution to the any of the other 88!

Thank you!

topics.title: Pre-algebra Problem
topics.text:
Three farmers are at the market. Farmer John sells $3$ carrots for $1$ dollar. Farmer Jihn sells $4$ carrots for $2$ dollars. Farmer Jahn sells $5$ carrots for $3$ dollars.

In the first hour, John sells $18$ carrots, Jihn sells $16$ carrots, and Jahn sells $5$ carrots. Jahn, who is very displeased with his sells, steals $5$ dollars from the other two people.

Then, another hour passes. John sells $21$ carrots, Jihn sells $4$ carrots, and Jahn sells $10$ carrots. Jihn, who is displeased, takes $4$ dollars from  the other two people.

Yet another hour passes! John sells $3$ carrots, Jihn sells $8$ carrots, and Jahn sells $15$ carrots. A displeased John takes $3$ dollars from Jihn and Jahn each.



This process repeats two more times. Then, sells return to normal, and John sells $18$ carrots, Jihn sells $18$ carrots, and Jahn sells $18$ carrots.



While walking home, a burglar takes $5$ dollars from each person.



After walking home, how many dollars does each person have? (Including the burglar.)

topics.title: 2017 State Team Round number 10
topics.text: In right triangle ABC, AB = 5, BC = 12 and AC = 13. P lies on side AC so that ray BP bisects angle ABC. Q and R lie on side BC so that BQ = QR = RC. Segments AQ and AR intersect segment BP at X and Y, respectively. What is the area of quadrilateral QRYX? Express your answer as a common fraction.

topics.title: Building a School Math Club
topics.text: Recently, a cool teacher from my middle school has offered to create a math club. I am PSYCHED, but since this has been our first time organizing a club like this, I would like some advice crafting our club. I'm personally in charge of gathering possible club members and have been wondering if we should offer a relatively simple screening test and whatnot. Any suggestions, advice, or resources in mind? (P.S. The teacher herself is a frequenter on AoPS and so we'll be doing extracurricular and/or competitive math.)
